speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy has made considerable progress toward our dual-mandate objectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased substantially over the past year, while the labor market has remained strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s very good news.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But inflation is still too high, further progress in bringing it down is not assured, and the path forward is uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are fully committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to achieve a sustainably strong labor market that benefits all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings, though at a slower pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our restrictive stance of monetary policy has been putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation, and the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals have moved toward better balance over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: However, in recent months, inflation has shown a lack of further progress toward our 2 percent objective, and we remain highly attentive to inflation risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has continued to expand at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although GDP growth moderated from 3.4 percent in the fourth quarter of last year to 1.6 percent in the first quarter, private domestic final purchases—which excludes inventory investment, government spending and net exports, and usually sends a clearer signal on underlying demand—was 3.1 percent in the first quarter, as strong as the second half of 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending has been robust over the past several quarters, even as high interest rates have weighed on housing and equipment investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Improving supply conditions have supported resilient demand and the strong performance of the U.S. economy over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market remains relatively tight, but supply and demand conditions have come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 276,000 jobs per month in the first quarter, while the unemployment rate remains low at 3.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Strong job creation over the past year has been accompanied by an increase in the supply of workers, reflecting increases in participation among individuals aged 25 to 54 years and a continued strong pace of immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has eased over the past year and the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed, but labor demand still exceeds the supply of available workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased notably over the past year but remains above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.7 percent over the 12 months ending in March; excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The inflation data received so far this year have been higher than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although some measures of short-term inflation expectations have increased in recent months, longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed’s monetary policy actions are guided by our mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship, as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are strongly committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee decided at today’s meeting to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent and to continue the process of significantly reducing our securities holdings, though at a slower pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past year, as labor market tightness has eased and inflation has declined, the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals have moved toward better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economic outlook is uncertain, however, and we remain highly attentive to inflation risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve stated that we do not expect that it will be appropriate to reduce the target range for the federal funds rate until we have gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So far this year, the data have not given us that greater confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In particular, and as I noted earlier, readings on inflation have come in above expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is likely that gaining such greater confidence will take longer than previously expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are prepared to maintain the current target range for the federal funds rate for as long as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re also prepared to respond to an unexpected weakening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too soon or too much could result in a reversal of the progress we’ve seen on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too late or too little could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering any adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Turning to our balance sheet: The Committee decided at today’s meeting to slow the pace of decline in our securities holdings, consistent with the plans we released previously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Specifically, the cap on Treasury redemptions will be lowered from the current $60 billion per month to $25 billion per month as of June 1.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consistent with the Committee’s intention to hold primarily Treasury securities in the longer run, we’re leaving the cap on agency securities unchanged per month, and we will reinvest any proceeds in excess of this cap in Treasury securities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With principal payments on agency securities currently running at about $15 billion per month, total portfolio runoff will amount to roughly $40 billion per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The decision to slow the pace of runoff does not mean that our balance sheet will ultimately shrink by less than it would otherwise but rather allows us to approach its ultimate level more gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In particular, slowing the pace of runoff will help ensure a smooth transition, reducing the possibility that money markets experience stress and thereby facilitating the ongoing decline in our securities holdings that are consistent with reaching the appropriate level of ample reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal and to keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to set the stage for achieving maximum employment and stable prices over the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, at the Fed, will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I do think the evidence shows, you know, pretty clearly that policy is restrictive and is weighing on demand, and there are a few places I would point to for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can start with the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So demand is still strong—the demand side of the labor market, in particular—but it’s cooled from its extremely high level of a couple years ago, and you see that in job openings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You saw it—more evidence of that today in the JOLTS report, as you’ll know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s still higher than pre-pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it has been coming down both in the Indeed report and the JOLTS report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s demand cooling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The same is true of quits and hiring rates, which have essentially normalized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You also see in interest-sensitive spending, like housing and investment—you also see that higher interest rates are weighing on those activities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I do think it’s clear that, that policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say that we believe it is restrictive, and we believe [that] over time it will be sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That will be a question that, that the data will have to answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Are anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I don’t want to get into complicated hypotheticals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say that, you know, we’re committed to retaining our current restrictive stance of policy for as long as is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it’s unlikely that the next policy rate move will be a hike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’d say it’s unlikely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, our policy focus is really what I just mentioned, which is—which is how long to keep policy restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think we’d need to see persuasive evidence that our policy stance is not sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation sustainably down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not—that’s not what we think we’re seeing, as I—as I mentioned, but that’s—something like that is what it would take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’d look at the totality of the data in answer to that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That would include inflation, inflation expectations, and all the other data too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I think, again, the test—what I’m saying is, if we were to come to that conclusion that policy weren’t tight enough to achieve that, so it would be the totality of all the things we’d be looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It could be expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It could be a combination of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, if we—if we reach that conclusion—and we don’t see evidence supporting that conclusion—that’s what it would take I think for us to take that step.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, on—let me address cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, obviously, our decisions that we make on our policy rate are going to depend on the incoming data, how the outlook is evolving, and the balance of risks, as always.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll look at the totality of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, and we think, that policy is well positioned to address different paths that the economy might take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve said that we don’t think it would be appropriate to dial back our restrictive policy stance until we’ve gained greater confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, for example, let me take a path: If we did have a path where inflation proves more persistent than expected and where the labor market remains strong, but inflation is moving sideways and we’re not gaining greater confidence, well, that would be a case in which it could be appropriate to hold off on rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think there’s also other paths that the economy could take, which, which would cause us to want to consider rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those would be—two of those paths would be that we do gain greater confidence, as we’ve said, that inflation is moving sustainably down to 2 percent, and another path could be, you know, an unexpected weakening in the labor market, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those are paths in which you could see us cutting rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it really will depend on the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of peak rate, you know, I think, really, it’s the same question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think the data will have to answer that question for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, it’s, it’s—we’ve set ourselves a test that we—for us to begin to reduce policy restriction, we’d want to be confident that inflation is moving—you know, moving sustainably down to 2 percent, and, for sure, one of the things we’d be looking at is the performance of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’d also be looking at inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’d be looking at the whole story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But clearly, incoming, incoming inflation data would be at the very heart of that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it’s hard to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’ll be able to look back, you know, from down the road and look back and understand it better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, if you look at—let’s look at growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Really, what we’ve seen so far this year in the first quarter is growth coming in about consistent with where it was last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I know GDP came in lower, but you don’t see an acceleration in growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, the thought would be that financial conditions loosened in, in, December, and that caused an uptick in activity, and that caused inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Presumably, that’s what we’re tightening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t really see that happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What you see is economic activity at a level that’s roughly the same as, as last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ll, we’ll have a better sense of that over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know that there’s an obvious connection there, though, with easing of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of tightening, you’re, you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Rates are certainly higher now and have been for some time than they were before the December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they’re higher, and that’s tighter financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, that’s appropriate, given what inflation has done in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I just want to be careful that we don’t target wage growth or the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And remember what we saw last year: very strong growth, a really tight labor market, and a historically fast decline in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and that’s because we know there are two forces at work here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s the unwinding of the pandemic-related supply-side distortions and demand-side distortions, and there’s also monetary policy, you know, restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t rule out that something like that can continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I wouldn’t give up, at this point, on further things happening on the supply side either because, you know, we do see that companies still report that there are supply-side issues that they’re facing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, even when the supply-side issues are solved, it should take some time for that to affect economic activity and ultimately inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there are still those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t like to say that either strong—either growth or, or a strong labor market, in and of itself, would automatically create problems on inflation, because, of course, it didn’t do that last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You ask about wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also don’t—we don’t target wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We target price inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is one of the inputs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The point with wages is, of course, we, like everyone else, like to see high wages, but we also want to see them not eaten up by high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s really what we’re trying to do, is to cool the economy and work with what’s happening on the supply side to bring—to bring the economy back to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Part of that will probably be having wage increases move down incrementally toward levels that are more sustainable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not really thinking of it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the—what we said is that we need to be more confident, and we’ve said—my colleagues and I today said that we didn’t see progress in the first—in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’ve said that it appears, then, that it’s going to take longer for us to reach that point of confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t know how long it’ll take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I can just say that when we get that confidence, then rate cuts will be in scope.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I don’t know exactly when that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I—you know, not really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, what, what—so I thought it was appropriate to reserve judgment until, until we had the full quarter’s data, until we saw the March data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so take a step back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see strong economic activity, we see a strong labor market, and we see inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see three inflation readings, and so I think you’re at a point there where you should take some signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t like to react to one or two months’ data, but this is a full quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think it’s appropriate to take signal now, and we are taking signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the signal that we’re taking is that it’s likely to take longer for us to gain confidence that we are on a sustainable path down to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the signal that we’re taking now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we will—you know, we will put the thing—we have put the thing under a microscope.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will say, nothing is going to come out of that that’s going to change the view.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that, in fact, we didn’t gain confidence and that it’s going to take longer to get that confidence—but—confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I just think—you know the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What’s happened since December is you’ve seen higher goods inflation than expected, and you’ve seen higher nonhousing services inflation than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those two are working together to, to sort of be higher than we had thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there are stories behind how that happened, and, you know, we—I think—I think my expectation is that we will, over the course of this year, see inflation move back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s my forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think my confidence in that is lower than it was because of the data that we’ve seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we’re looking at those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also continue to expect, and I continue to expect, that housing services inflation, given where market rents are, those will show up in measured housing services inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, on your first question, I don’t have a probability estimate for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But all I can say is that, you know, we’ve said that we didn’t think it would be appropriate to cut until we were more confident that inflation was moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t get our confidence, in that [it] didn’t increase in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, in fact, what really happened was we came to the view that it will take longer to get that confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think there are—you know, I think it’s—the economy has been very hard for forecasters broadly to predict—to predict its path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there are paths to, to not cutting, and there are paths to cutting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s really going to depend on the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of the employment mandate, to your point, if you go back a couple of years, our, our sort of framework document says that, when you look at the two mandate goals, and if one of them is further away from goal than the other, then you focus on that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It actually—it’s the time to get back there times the, you know, times how far it is from the goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that was clearly inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So our focus was very much on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As—and this is what we referred to in the statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I don’t have great confidence in which of those paths—I think I would say my personal forecast is that we will begin to see further progress on inflation this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think I would take that question this way: We saw a year of very high productivity growth in 2023, and we saw a year of, I think, negative productivity growth in 2022.

sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we, we believe our policy stance is in a good place and is appropriate to the current situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We believe it’s restrictive, and, you know, we—our evidence for that, I went over earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see it in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see it in inflation-sensitive spending, where demand has clearly come down a lot over the past few years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s more from monetary policy, whereas the supply side of things that are happening are more on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how I would think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, of course we’re not satisfied with 3 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: “Three percent” can’t be in a sentence with “satisfied.” [Laughter] So we will return inflation to 2 percent over time but over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think our policy stance is, is appropriate to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if we were to conclude that policy is not sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation sustainably down to 2 percent, then that would be what it would take for us to want to increase rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t see evidence for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the policy focus has been on—has really been on what to do about, about holding the current—the current level of restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really—that’s part of the policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where the policy discussion was in the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There isn’t any rule.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can’t look to a rule.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, these are—these are going to be judgment calls.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, clearly restrictive monetary policy needs more time to do its job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That, that is pretty clear, based on what we’re seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: How long that will take and how patient we should be is going to depend on the totality of the data, how the outlook evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re, we’re always going to do what we think the right thing for the economy is when we come to that consensus view that it’s the right thing to do for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s our record.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not looking at anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s hard enough to get the economics right here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These are difficult things, and if, if we were to take on a whole, another, set of factors and use that as a new filter, it would reduce the likelihood we’d actually get the economics right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how we think about it around here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re at peace over it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that we’ll do what we think is the right thing, when we think it’s the right thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll all do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, that’s how everybody around here thinks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I can’t say it enough, that we just don’t—we just don’t go down that road.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and so we’re not on that road.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re on the road where we’re serving all the American people and making our decisions based on the data and how those data affect the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s— VICTORIA GUIDA.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: An economic difference.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: —a significant difference between an institution that takes into account all sorts of political events and one that doesn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where the significant difference is, and, you know, we’re—we just don’t do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, you can go back and read the transcripts for every—this is my fourth election, fourth presidential election here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Read all the transcripts, and see if anybody mentions, in any way, the pending election.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just isn’t part of our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not what we’re hired to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we start down that road, again, I don’t know how you stop.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think if you go back to where wages peaked—wage increases peaked a couple, three years ago—essentially all wage measures have come down substantially [when compared] to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they are not, not down to where they were before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re still roughly a percentage point higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve seen pretty consistent progress but not uniformly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you’ll note the ECI reading from Tuesday was—it was expected to be—to have come down, and, essentially, it was flat year over year, you know, I think roughly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So yeah, I mean, it’s—that part of it is bumpy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, we don’t target wage increases, but, you know, in the longer run, if you have—if you have wage increases running higher than productivity would warrant, then, you know, there will be inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Employers will raise prices over time if that’s the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve seen progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has been inconsistent, but we have seen a substantial decline overall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we have a ways to go on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, the thing that hurts everybody, and particularly people in the lower-income brackets, is inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you’re a person who’s living paycheck to paycheck, and suddenly all the things you buy—the fundamentals of life—go up in price, you, you are in trouble right away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, with those people in mind, in particular, what we’re doing is, we’re using our tools to bring down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It will take some time, but we will succeed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we will bring inflation back down to 2 percent, and then people won’t have to worry about it again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’re doing, and we know that it’s painful and inconvenient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the dividends will be paid and will be very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and everyone will share in those dividends, and we’ve made quite a lot of progress if you can think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think core—I think headline—core PCE [inflation] peaked at 5.8 [percent].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now it’s at—anyway, headline peaked at 7.1.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now it’s at 2.7.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t want to get that wrong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I think—I think that restrictive monetary policy is doing what it’s supposed to do, and it’s—but it’s also, in this case unusually, working alongside and with the healing of the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This, this—what was different this time was that a big part of the source of the inflation and the reason why we’re having this conversation is that we had this supply-side kind of collapse, with shortages and bottlenecks and all that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so—and this was to do with the shutting down and reopening of the economy and other things that, that really raised demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, many factors did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think now you see those two things working together, the reversal of those supply and demand distortions from the pandemic and the response to it, along with restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those two things are working to bring down inflation, and we’ve made a lot of progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let’s remember how far we’ve come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we have a ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got work left to do, but we’re not looking at the very high inflation rates that we were seeing two years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, essentially, there are—there are a number of places in the economy where there are just lag structures built into the inflation process, and housing is one of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So when you have—when, when someone goes to—a new person goes to rent an apartment, that’s called market rent, and you can see market rents are barely going up at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The inflation in those has been very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it takes—before that, they were incredibly high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They sort of led the, the high part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what happens is, those market rents take years, actually, to get all the way into rents for tenants who are rolling over their leases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Landlords don’t tend to charge as much of an increase to a rollover tenant, for whatever reason.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what that does is it builds up a sort of an unrealized portion of increases when there have been big increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what happens is, you know—it’s complicated, but the story is it just takes some time for that to get in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now I am confident that, as long as market rents remain low, this is going to show up in measured inflation, assuming that market rents do remain low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’ve learned that the lags are longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We now think significantly longer than we thought at the beginning, and so confident that it will come but not so confident in the timing of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, yes, I expect that, that this will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that—you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think the difference between the United States and other countries that are now considering rate cuts is that they’re just not having the kind of growth we’re having.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They have—their inflation is performing about like ours or maybe a little better, but they’re not experiencing the kind of growth we’re experiencing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we actually have the luxury of having strong growth and a strong labor market, very low unemployment, high job creation, and all of that, and we can be patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we will—we’ll be careful and cautious as we approach the decision to cut rates, whereas I think other jurisdictions may go before that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of the implications, you know, I think obviously markets see it coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s priced in now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so I think the markets and economies can adapt to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think, you know, we haven’t seen—in addition, for the emerging market economies, we haven’t seen the kind of turmoil that was more frequent 20 years ago, 30 years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, I think, partly because emerging market countries, many of them have much better monetary policy frameworks, much more credibility on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so they’re navigating this pretty well this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we thought, and most people thought, there would have to be probably significant dislocations somewhere in the economy, perhaps the labor market, to get inflation all the way down from the very high levels it was at at the beginning of this episode.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That didn’t happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a tremendous result.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re very, of course, gratified and pleased that that hasn’t happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, if you look at the dynamics that enabled that, it really was that this, the—that so much of the gain was from the unwinding of things that weren’t to do with monetary policy but the unwinding of the distortions to the economy, you know, supply problems—supply-side problems and also some, some demand issues as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unwinding of those really helped inflation come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, as I’ve said, I’m not giving up on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think—I think it is possible that, that those forces will still work to help us bring inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can’t—we can’t be guaranteed that that’s true, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’re—you know, we’re trying to use our tools in a way that keeps the labor market strong, and the economy strong, but also helps bring inflation back down to 2 percent sustainably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will bring inflation down to 2 percent sustainably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We hope we can do it without, you know, without significant dislocations in the labor market or elsewhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I said “an unexpected weakening” is what I—the way I characterized it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know—and I’m not going to try to define exactly what I mean by that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, it would be—it would have to be meaningful and get our attention and lead us to think that the labor market was really significantly weakening for us to want to react to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A couple of tenths in the unemployment rate would be—would probably not do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But a broader—it would be a broader thing that would—that would suggest that it would be appropriate to consider cutting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think whether you decide to cut will depend on all the facts and circumstances, not just that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me—let me start by saying that the Fed is committed to, you know, completing this process and carrying out Basel III Endgame in a way that’s faithful to Basel and also comparable to what the other large comparable jurisdictions are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t made any decisions on, on policy or on process at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nothing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nothing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No decisions have been made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll say again, though, if we conclude that re-proposal is appropriate, we won’t hesitate to insist on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, there’s no mechanical rule in place there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say that the, you know, the Basel III process is by far the most important thing and really is, I think, occupying us at this time in terms of what’s, what’s—what we’re moving ahead with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think if you listen to, and you all do, listen to my 18 colleagues on the FOMC, you’ll see that we do not lack for a diversity of voices and perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We really don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s one of the great aspects of the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have 12 Reserve Banks around the country where they have their own economic staff, not the people who work here at the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are different people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, and so each, each Reserve Bank has its own culture around monetary policy and its own approach and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It guarantees you a diversity of perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that the perspectives are very diverse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—and, in terms of—in terms of dissents, you know, we have dissents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, a thoughtful dissent is a good thing, if someone really makes you think, that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But all I can say from my standpoint is I try—I listen carefully to people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I try to incorporate their thinking or do everything I can to incorporate their thinking into what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think many people, if they feel that’s happening, you know, that for most people most of the time, that’ll be enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And—but I’m not—I mean, it’s, it’s not, you know, frowned upon or illegal or against the rules or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It just is the way things come out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I mean, I think we have a very diverse group of rounded people—frankly, more diverse than it used to be in many dimensions, more diverse from the obvious gender and demographic ways, but also we have more people who are not Ph.D. economists.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have people from business and law and academia and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we actually do have quite a good diverse perspective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think all of us read these stories about the lack of diversity, and we look around the room and say, “I don’t understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I really don’t understand what they’re talking about.” So—but I get the question, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you very much.
